theme: Blessed is the man, the two ways
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 1. It is the gateway to the whole book of Psalms, and its picture of a tree by streams of water returns in the last chapter of the Bible. Notice the two ways, the two destinies, and the one who delights in God’s law.
settingTheScene: Psalm 1 has no title. It stands as the introduction to the Psalter, setting out the choice that all of the other psalms assume: there are two ways to live, and they lead to two ends. It reads like a wisdom poem, in the tradition of Proverbs and Deuteronomy 30. We now return to it as we begin the last book of the Bible, where the same two ways appear for the last time, in the tree of life and in the judgment of the wicked.
observation: “Blessed is the man who walks not in the counsel of the wicked, nor stands in the way of sinners, nor sits in the seat of scoffers” (v. 1).
“But his delight is in the law of the LORD, and on his law he meditates day and night” (v. 2).
“He is like a tree planted by streams of water that yields its fruit in its season” (v. 3).
“In all that he does, he prospers” (v. 3).
“The wicked are not so, but are like chaff that the wind drives away” (v. 4).
“Therefore the wicked will not stand in the judgment” (v. 5).
“For the LORD knows the way of the righteous” (v. 6).
“But the way of the wicked will perish” (v. 6).
interpretation:
The first word is “Blessed,” meaning deeply, lastingly happy. The blessed man is first described by what he avoids. Notice the progression: he walks, then stands, then sits. First he takes the counsel of the wicked, then he stands in the way of sinners, then he settles into the seat of scoffers. Sin starts as a casual step and becomes a way of life. The blessed person refuses to start down that road.

What he does instead is delight in God’s law: “on his law he meditates day and night.” The word “law” is torah, God’s instruction, and it points to the whole of God’s revealed word. Delight means that it is not merely a duty; it is a pleasure. Meditation means that he turns it over and over, as a cow chews the cud. The result is a picture of stability and fruit: “He is like a tree planted by streams of water that yields its fruit in its season, and its leaf does not wither.” The tree is planted, not wild; its roots reach the water; it does not wither in drought. “In all that he does, he prospers.” This is not a promise of worldly wealth for everyone who reads the Bible; it is a description of a life that, in God’s sight, succeeds and bears lasting fruit. Jeremiah 17:7-8 uses the same image.

By contrast, “The wicked are not so.” They are like chaff, the weightless husk the wind blows away. They have no roots, no fruit, no future. “Therefore the wicked will not stand in the judgment, nor sinners in the congregation of the righteous.” The psalm ends with the reason: “For the LORD knows the way of the righteous, but the way of the wicked will perish.” God knows, which means he watches over and cares for the way of the righteous, as in the phrase “The LORD knows those who are his.”

Reading this psalm in the light of Christ, we see that he is the truly blessed man. He alone never walked in the counsel of the wicked, and his delight was in the law of the LORD (Psalm 40:8). He is the tree whose fruit never fails. And in Revelation 22:2, the tree of life stands by the river of the water of life, bearing twelve kinds of fruit, with leaves for the healing of the nations. Those who are in Christ are planted by the streams of water, and one day will eat of that tree. The two ways of Psalm 1 are the two ways of the whole Bible, and the last chapters of Revelation show where each ends.
connection: Jeremiah 17:7-8 uses the image of a tree by water. Joshua 1:8 commands meditating on the law day and night. Psalm 119 is an extended meditation on the law. Deuteronomy 30:15-20 sets before Israel life and death. Proverbs 4:14-19 describes two paths. Matthew 7:13-14 speaks of the two ways. Psalm 40:6-8 and Hebrews 10:5-9 show Christ delighting to do God’s will. John 15:1-8 speaks of abiding and bearing fruit. Genesis 2:9 and Revelation 2:7, 22:2 mention the tree of life. Matthew 3:12 speaks of chaff.
application:
Ask what counsel you have been listening to, and where you may be starting to “walk, stand, or sit” in a place you should not.

Choose a short passage and meditate on it throughout the day. Return to it when you have a spare moment.

Thank Christ that he is the blessed man in your place, and that his roots reach to the stream of life.
prayerPrompts: Tell God you want to be blessed as his word describes.
Ask him to keep you from the counsel of the wicked.
Ask him to root you in his word.
